headline: Government shutdowns usually have little economic impact. This time could be different
summary: For all the political firestorms they generate, government shutdowns have been nonevents for both markets and the economy.
content_truncated:
A view of the U.S. Capitol on September 29, 2025 in Washington, DC. 
For all the political firestorms they generate, government shutdowns historically have been nonevents for both markets and the ec… [+4023 chars]
full_text:
For all the political firestorms they generate, government shutdowns historically have been nonevents for both markets and the economy.
This time, though, could be different.
That's because President Donald Trump's threat to make some federal government furloughs resulting from the shutdown permanent could have longer-lasting impacts on an employment picture that already has been looking precarious.
Should Trump follow through on the threat — and successfully weather what almost certainly would be yet another court challenge to his executive authority — it throws a wrench into what otherwise have been much more political than economic events.
"We have reason to think that a shutdown this time may not follow past precedent," Michael McLean, public policy senior analyst at Barclays, said in a client note. If Trump follows through, "this would be a significant departure from past practice and could inject new uncertainty into the economic effect of a shutdown, which otherwise we would expect to be marginal."
Indeed, shutdowns in the past have left little mark other than the political damage done to the party perceived as at fault.
Markets have sold off on occasion but then quickly recovered. For growth, most economists calculate the impact as about 0.1 percentage point off gross domestic product for week. Being that the longest closure lasted 35 days, from-late 2018 until the following January, that's not a lot for a $30 trillion economy. The short-term losses are usually easily recouped in subsequent quarters, according to Bank of America.
Labor market trouble
However, in this case the labor market already has been wobbly. In particular, the Washington, D.C. region, where a large share of federal government employees call home, has taken a hit from the layoffs earlier this year advocated by Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency advisory board.
Shutdowns automatically mean that employees not deemed essential are furloughed, but are always summoned back once the impasse ends. Trump threatened, in an NBC News interview Sunday, that "we are going to cut a lot of the people that ... we're able to cut on a permanent basis."
The impact on the monthly nonfarm payrolls report wouldn't show up until the October count is released in November, where Trump's threat "could have a more severe near-term impact" than usual, wrote Nomura economist David Seif.
But that brings up another wrinkle: Should the shutdown last any significant amount of time, it could delay the release of key economic data.
Impact on the BLS
The Labor Department said Friday it will shut down virtually all activity. The department's Bureau of Labor Statistics, which releases multiple key economic reports including the monthly jobs count, would be shuttered as long as the shutdown lasts. In an action plan to address the situation, the department warned of delays and also said a "reduction in quality" for the data could occur.
For Social Security recipients, a delay in the release of the consumer price index inflation reading could impact cost-of-living adjustments.
The situation also could impact the Federal Reserve, which relies on BLS data when making its decisions on interest rates and other matters relating to monetary policy.
"While the US government may be headed for a shutdown, we expect little economic impact," Mark Cabana, head of rates strategy at Bank of America, said in a note. "A shutdown would pause economic data releases, leaving the Fed reliant on private data for its policy decisions if the shutdown extends."
One corollary would be the 2013 shutdown, when the September jobs report was delayed until Oct. 22. That month's CPI also was postponed by two weeks.
Elizabeth Renter, senior economist at NerdWallet, concurred with most Wall Street analyses in that the ultimate impact should be "relatively mild." However, she noted the potential hit to the labor market.
"The most immediate and impactful effect is on furloughed federal employees and contractors," she said. "When households are forced to go without income, even for a week, it can set back their financial stability significantly."

headline: Charlie Javice sentenced to 7 years in prison in JPMorgan Chase fraud case
summary: A federal judge in Manhattan has sentenced the former fintech wunderkind to a 7-year prison sentence.
content_truncated: Charlie Javice arriving at a lower Manhattan federal courthouse for her sentencing hearing. Javice was found guilty of fraud for artificially inflating her customer numbers while selling her company … [+5239 chars]
full_text:
- Charlie Javice was sentenced to 7 years in prison for tricking JPMorgan into paying $175M for her startup.
- Javice was convicted of fraud in March for lying that her website, Frank, had 4 million Gen-Z users.
- In fact, her student financial aid platform never had more than 300,000 users.
Charlie Javice is going to prison for the better part of a decade.
On Monday, a Manhattan federal judge sentenced Javice to seven years in prison for using wildly exaggerated data to fool JPMorgan Chase into paying $175 million for her startup — far more than the 18 months her lawyers asked for.
Javice's prison sentence will be followed by 3 years of supervised release, resulting in a total 10-year sentence. The judge ordered her to report to prison 60 days after she exhausts her appeals to higher courts.
The former fintech wunderkind — who once graced Forbes' 30 Under 30 list and scored a one-on-one meeting with JPMC's powerful CEO, Jamie Dimon, during the 2021 sale negotiations — must also pay millions in restitution and forfeiture.
US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein ordered Javice to forfeit over $22 million in ill-gotten salary, stock, and bonuses she received for selling the company and working for a year as a managing director before the fraud was uncovered.
Javice must also share with her co-defendant Olivier Amar the burden of paying $287.5 million in restitution — the Frank sale price, plus more than $100 million that JP Morgan Chase was obligated under bank bylaws to pay them in legal fees.
Hellerstein gave some credit to Javice's own emotional courtroom comments earlier in the sentencing hearing, and to the letters submitted by friends and family who spoke to her good character. The judge said Javice's crimes "required a great deal of duplicity," but that she was "a good person who has done good deeds."
"I don't think you will be committing any crimes, and I think you will be devoting your life to service," Hellerstein told Javice in the lower Manhattan courtroom. "But others need to be deterred."
Javice's family members appeared relieved by the sentence. Following the hearing, they shared smiles and embraces — and declined to comment to the press in the hallway.
Javice was convicted in March of conspiracy, wire, and bank fraud for using bogus user-base data to claim Frank — a platform that streamlined the federal financial aid application process, along with offering career and financial advice — had stockpiled the contact information for 4 million users. In fact, Frank never had data for more than 300,000 users.
Fighting back tears at Monday's sentencing hearing, Javice, who is 32, said she wishes she could tell her younger self to take a different path.
"At 28, I did something that runs against the grain of my upbringing and every lesson I once claimed to have learned," she said in the courtroom.
She implored forgiveness from JP Morgan investors whom she defrauded and from Frank employees and investors "whose name, career, or future was in some way stained by proximity to me."
"Not a day goes by that I do not replay my mistakes, searching for meaning," Javice said. "Not a day passes that I do not feel profound remorse."
The Frank fraud
Prosecutors in the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York had sought a 12-year prison sentence and $300 million in restitution.
The hefty sum would compensate for the "enormous victim loss," prosecutors argued.
Prosecutors said Javice pocketed $29 million of the $175 million Frank sale herself, while her defense lawyers put the figure closer to $21 million.
JPMorgan Chase had seen great marketing potential in Frank's massive database of 4 million users, according to trial testimony.
The bank wanted to use the contact information to pitch checking accounts, credit cards, and other banking products to college-age users at the start of their lifelong financial journeys.
"Based on the defendant's lies, JPMC projected it could generate more than $500 million in revenue from selling banking products to Frank's customers," prosecutors argued.
"Had JPMC known the truth — that Frank had only a few hundred thousand users — the bank would not have acquired Frank," they wrote.
Javice had hoped to get a break in both prison time and restitution by admitting wrongdoing and trying to convince the judge that the acquisition was not a complete loss for JP Morgan.
"Regardless of the number of users, Frank had real value," her lawyers argued pre-sentencing.
Hellerstein had little patience with an argument from Javice's lawyers that he should take into account JPMorgan's mistake in buying Frank. According to Javice's attorney Ronald Sullivan Jr. JPMorgan made a mistake by rushing to purchase the startup before a competitor could buy it.
"A fraud remains a fraud whether you outsmart someone who is smart or someone who is a fool," Hellerstein said.
At the same time, Hellerstein declined to force Javice to pay restitution for the legal fees JP Morgan says they paid to discover the fraud, saying it was part of the price of doing business.
Hellerstein also rebutted Javice's claim that she deserved a sentencing break for admitting she did something wrong.
"She said she made a mistake," the judge said of her letter to him. "She doesn't admit she committed a crime. I don't think it's an acceptance of responsibility."
In Monday's sentencing hearing, Sullivan praised Javice's good deeds that "were not in the newspapers" and implored the judge to take them into consideration.
According to Sullivan — citing a sheaf of letters from family, friends, and acquaintances who wrote to support Javice — the Frank founder assisted seriously ill family members, quietly paid grocery bills for people who were struggling, and gave opportunities to people who are traditionally excluded from certain career paths.
"We think that that is more in line with what is fair for a woman who has done good for most of her life," Sullivan said.
Near the end of the hearing Monday, Hellerstein permitted Javice to stay out of prison while she appeals her case, which her lawyers said would be done speedily. But he paused to ask whether Javice, a dual French-US citizen, might flee to escape her seven-year prison sentence.
"I intend to stay here and serve my sentence with dignity," Javice told him.
The judge appeared assured by comments from her lawyers, who said that her personal ties were in the United States.
"I am convinced that she will not flee — that her life is here," Hellerstein said.

headline: Bad Bunny Headlining Super Bowl Signals A New Era In Marketing
summary: The NFL’s Super Bowl choice of Bad Bunny highlights shifting demographics and offers brands lessons on growth, representation, and cultural relevance.
content_truncated: SAN JUAN, PUERTO RICO - JULY 11: Bad Bunny performs onstage during Night One of Bad Bunny: "No Me Quiero Ir De Aqui" Residencia En El Choli at Coliseo de Puerto Rico José Miguel Agrelot on July 11, 2… [+5306 chars]
full_text:
Bad Bunny will headline the Super Bowl halftime show in 2026. Many fans are rejoicing for the selection, even though there is some backlash from others. When you look at the details from a marketing perspective, the choice just makes sense.
Latinos are the fastest-growing fanbase for the NFL. Viewership among both English and Spanish speaking fans is up 11%. Broadcasts of NFL games in Spanish have spiked 34% in comparison to recent years. And the NFL has been cultivating a global fan base, as part of its plans for global expansion for years. The plan includes playing seven games in countries Europe and South America, and and expanding to play a game in Australia during the 2026 season.
Record breaking artist Bad Bunny has fans all around the world. He’s kicking off the rest of his global tour after his ground-breaking 31-show residency in Puerto Rico that pumped more than $4 million into the islands economy. His last show in Puerto Rico was streamed live on Amazon Music and broke records for live streaming viewership. In 2022, his album was the first all-Spanish album to reach number one in the U.S. And in 2024, his music was the third most streamed in the world behind Taylor Swift and The Weeknd.
While fans are in for an experience, for what promises to be a ground breaking show, the announcement just provides another data point of many that highlights a shift in the way marketers should be approaching growing their brands.
Growth Requires Reaching A Broader Customer Base
Like many brands, the NFL has been focused on growth. The organization’s playbook includes creating programming and opportunities to invite new fans to the sport, establish and nurture relationships with them and their communities, and removing any friction to them becoming lifelong fans.
That programming includes the International Player Pathway Program to support and develop players from around the world in their quest to play in the NFL. The league’s focus on flag football has supported them in creating a large and growing fanbase of women and girls. And of course, the league has committed to playing NFL games in different cities around the world to deepen fandom.
For your brand to continue to grow, you’ll need to work to diversify your customer base as well. Doing that effectively, goes beyond simply adding representative imagery in your promotional campaigns.
The NFL choosing Bad Bunny to headline the Super Bowl halftime show is just another lever to accomplish their growth goals, by tapping into the artists global appeal.
Growing new communities of consumers will require your brand to invest in relevant forms of customer acquisition for the consumers you want to reach, and enhancing your customer experience throughout to ensure they feel like they belong with you at every touchpoint.
The New General Market Demands Better Representation
The consumers you want to serve need to see themselves and or who they aspire to be reflected in the visual imagery your brand puts forth. The NFL has been courting Latino consumers for years now.
It only makes sense that the brand represents that fan base in a meaningful way. Bad Bunny is a conduit for that.
But even more than just featuring talent from the Latino community to court the community, the NFL is also leaning into a shift from the “historical general market” to the “new general market.”
It is representing not only what they want their customer base to be, but also what the population already is.
In the U.S., the Hispanic population represents 19.5% of the population. One in four children in the U.S. are Hispanic, showing continued growth.
As such it becomes a liability for a brand to not represent, in mainstream media and marketing such a large percentage of the population and your ideal customer.
The NFL is reflecting demographic shifts in the imagery they put forth and who they choose to feature. Your brand should do the same.
Consumers Are Done With Assimilation
Bad Bunny’s music is almost entirely in Spanish. As an artist, he is unapologetic about releasing music in Spanish, and staying true to his culture and heritage. And when many artists have assimilated and produced music in English as a way to advance their careers, Bad Bunny has made an intentional choice to not do that. He’ll be headlining the world’s biggest music stage, so it is clear that assimilating to English-speaking culture hasn’t hindered his impact or superstardom.
Consumers are internalizing a similar attitude. Gone are the days where consumers on the whole felt like they needed to hide or downplay what made them different, for the purpose of achieving success, not rocking the boat, or to feel like they fit in.
These days, consumers are more interested in finding brands and spaces where they belong. Where they can show up as they are, be accepted for who they are, and accepted and celebrated for who they are.
And these consumers now have the expectation that the brands they engage with and buy from, will not only just acknowledge their identity, but create products, experiences, and communications the clearly and quickly demonstrate that the brands sees, and supports them, and wants them to be a customer — as they are.
For your brand to succeed with today’s consumer, it is important to acknowledge and embrace the differences of the people you want to serve.

summary: Charlie Javice, founder of college financial aid platform Frank, was arrested in 2023 on charges she defrauded JPMorgan Chase in the sale of the fintech firm.
content_truncated:
Charlie Javice, founder of a startup acquired by JPMorgan Chase in 2021 for $175 million, is facing sentencing Monday for defrauding the bank by overstating how many customers the fintech firm had.
… [+3013 chars]
full_text:
Charlie Javice, founder of a startup acquired by JPMorgan Chase in 2021 for $175 million, was sentenced to just over seven years in prison Monday for defrauding the bank by overstating how many customers the fintech firm had.
In March, a 12-person jury found Javice and her chief growth officer Olivier Amar guilty on three counts of fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit fraud. Prosecutors had sought a sentence of 12 years.
Javice, 33, cried as she delivered an emotional statement to the court Monday. Standing to address the judge, Javice said she felt profound remorse for her actions and asked for forgiveness from JPMorgan, employees of the startup, shareholders and investors.
At one point, Javice turned and directly addressed her family, sitting in the front row, to apologize and thank them for what she called unwavering support.
"I will spend my entire life regretting these errors," Javice said.
"I'm asking with all of my heart for forgiveness," she said. "I ask your Honor to temper justice with mercy … I will accept your judgment with dignity and humility."
Judge Alvin Hellerstein told Javice her words were "very moving" and that the way she's devoted her life is "highly commendable," but that he couldn't give her the forgiveness she sought.
"I sentence people not because they're bad, but because they do bad things," Hellerstein told Javice before delivering the 85-month prison sentence. "I don't think you'll be committing other crimes and that you'll be devoting your life to service, but others have to be deterred."
In addition to prison, Javice was sentenced to three years of supervision, along with $22.36 million in forfeiture and $287 million in restitution to JPMorgan. She will remain out on bail while she appeals the ruling.
JPM acquisition
JPMorgan bought the startup, called Frank, to help the biggest U.S. bank by assets market its financial products to students. Frank was a digital platform that helped students apply for financial aid. In September 2021, JPMorgan told CNBC in an exclusive interview on the deal that the fintech firm had served more than five million students since Javice founded it.
But months after the deal closed, JPMorgan discovered that Frank had fewer than 300,000 real customers; the rest were synthetic identities created by Javice with the help of a data scientist.
Javice was arrested in 2023 on charges that she defrauded JPMorgan in the deal. Details that emerged later showed that Frank employees expressed disbelief when Javice directed them to boost their customer roster before the acquisition.
The week before selling her company to JPMorgan, Javice directed an employee to fabricate millions of users. When the employee declined, Javice reassured him, according to testimony given earlier this year.
"She said: 'Don't worry. I don't want to end up in an orange jumpsuit,'" the employee testified.
Not Theranos
On Monday, Javice's attorney Ronald Sullivan argued for a lighter sentence for his client, making the case that Frank helped customers. He contrasted the case against that of Elizabeth Holmes of Theranos infamy, whose fraud he said had "dangerous medical consequences," and who was sentenced to 135 months in prison.
"Ms. Javice's sentence should be nowhere near Elizabeth Holmes,'" Sullivan told Judge Hellerstein.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Micah Fergenson disagreed, arguing that Javice's crime was fueled by greed.
"JPMorgan didn't get a functioning business, they acquired a crime scene," Fergenson said.
The episode was embarrassing for JPMorgan, which was thought to be one of the most sophisticated of corporate acquirers. Concerned about threats from fintech and big tech firms, the bank, led by CEO Jamie Dimon, went on a shopping spree of smaller fintech firms starting in 2020.
But JPMorgan, eager to edge out rivals bidding for the startup, failed to confirm that Frank actually had millions of customers before shelling out $175 million for the company.

The model is better at coding, using computers and meeting practical business needs, and it excels in specialized fields like cybersecurity, finance and research, Anthropic said. The Amazon-backed startup, which is valued at $183 billion, is making Claude Sonnet 4.5 available to all users.
Anthropic said Claude Sonnet 4.5 is the "best coding model in the world" according to industry benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified, a test set that measures an AI system's software coding abilities.
"People are just noticing with this model, because it's just smarter and more of a colleague, that it's kind of fun to work with it when encountering problems and fixing them," Jared Kaplan, Anthropic's co-founder and chief science officer, told CNBC in an interview.
The model generates higher-quality code, is better at identifying code improvements and can follow instructions more reliably, the company said.
Claude Sonnet 4.5 comes after Anthropic launched Claude Opus 4.1 in August and Claude Sonnet 4 in May. It's the latest example of the breakneck pace of innovation within the AI industry.
Anthropic was founded by a group of former OpenAI researchers in 2021, and the two companies have been fierce competitors ever since.
OpenAI kick-started the generative artificial intelligence boom following the release of its ChatGPT chatbot in 2022. The startup, which has seen its valuation swell to $500 billion, announced its latest model, GPT-5, in August. The rollout was rocky, as some users complained about losing access to the company's prior models.
Mike Krieger, Anthropic's chief product officer, said that Claude Sonnet 4.5 will be the default for users and that Anthropic recommends the model for "basically every use case."
Even so, users will have options. Paid subscribers can still choose to use Opus, and users with specific workflows can select an older generation of Sonnet if they aren't ready to migrate overnight, he said.
Claude Sonnet 4.5 is smaller than Claude Opus 4.1 but smarter than it in "almost every single way," Krieger added.
"We have found it, and our customers are finding it, very useful for real, actual work," Krieger said.
Claude Sonnet 4.5 can run autonomously for 30 hours, and Anthropic said it's able to maintain focus on complex, multistep tasks throughout that period. Claude Opus 4, which the company launched in May, could run autonomously for just seven hours.
Anthropic has also been able to improve the model's behavior through extensive safety training, the company said. It has reduced "concerning behaviors" like deception, power seeking and sycophancy, which is when a model tells a user what they want to hear.
Claude Sonnet 4.5 is also more resistant to prompt injection attacks, where a model can get tricked into doing something malicious, like exposing sensitive data.
"This is the biggest jump in safety that I think we've seen in the last probably year, year and a half," Kaplan said.
Additional model launches are already on the horizon for Anthropic. Kaplan said better models are coming, including "very likely Opus."
"No promises," he said. "But I think that we'll probably have one or two more releases before the end of the year."

full_text:
Reported by Francesca Walton
DAY 1
Welcome to the 30 Under 30 Summit
Welcome to our coverage of the 12th annual Forbes Under 30 Summit. Since 2014, Forbes has hosted this gathering as a way for young leaders and new entrepreneurs to network, learn from the best entrepreneurial minds, and find new business opportunities.
This year’s event is happening in Columbus, Ohio, from September 28 to October 1. As always, festivities kicked off with the Forbes Under 30 Concert. First on deck, indie-electronic musical duo Forester warmed up the crowd. With over 200 million streams, their songs combine the feelings of natural landscapes with the energy of city life. Up next, Alex Warren, the 25-year-old singer and songwriter responsible for one of 2025’s songs of the summer (“Ordinary”) performed his chart-topping hit. And Lucy Guo, the world’s youngest self-made billionaire by way of her work in AI, took the stage to showcase another one of her talents: DJing. It was electric.
Guo will rejoin the Under 30 stage on Monday as one of our featured speakers; so too will Olympian Suni Lee, former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, Poppi founder Allison Ellsworth, along with many more.
Opening Remarks
J.P. Nauseef, the president and CEO of JobsOhio, opened the first morning of programming by welcoming the audiences to the Battelle Grand—which had been transformed from a convention into a multi-room event space featuring a main stage, upper-deck viewing areas, Under 30-themes cafes, a game day announcer-style podcast studio and more. After taking a selfie with the crowd, who he called “the best of the brightest,” he broke down the benefits of living in Ohio, particularly Columbus, and why it’s a “great place for you to build your business.”
Following opening remarks from Nauseef, Randall Lane, the chief content officer at Forbes and the founder of the Forbes 30 Under 30 List, took the stage. Lane talked about his own business experience—the difficulties he faced when fundraising for his own ventures, and how he needed a community to share ideas with. That is why Forbes is so excited to bring this group together: “It’s the greatest gathering of young entrepreneurs in the world,” said Lane. “Lean in and learn… This is a new golden age of entrepreneurship.”
From Founder To Presidential Candidate: An Under 30 Alum’s Vision For America
Randall Lane was joined on stage by former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. A little over 10 years ago, in 2014, Ramaswamy made it onto the 30 Under 30 list for his work co-managing Roivant Sciences, a large biotech-focused portfolio business. The company went public in 2021 in a $3 billion IPO; today, he stands as one of the youngest people on the Forbes World’s Billionaires list with an estimated net worth of $1.2 billion.
In 2021, Ramaswamy stepped down as the CEO of Roivant and turned his attention to politics, writing a book called “Woke, Inc.” that lambasts the way corporate America has, in Ramaswamy’s opinion, become absorbed in social justice and ESG issues. In 2024, he ran for president but dropped his bid to back Donald Trump. The biotech billionaire is now running for governor in his home state of Ohio, following his departure from the Department of Government Efficiency, also known as DOGE.
Ramaswamy is focused on cultivating the younger generation of Americans. They are the ones who have “skin in the game,” he said Monday. And they are the ones at the front of this “new frontier for American unity.” Lane asked Ramaswamy about cohesion in America and how the left and right can come together. The solution is “more conversation, not less,” Ramaswamy said. “There must be a commitment to disagree and respect each other.”
As a good friend of Charlie Kirk, the right-wing political activist and cofounder of Turning Point USA who was recently assassinated at a Utah college event, Ramaswamy believes in the importance of free speech, “speaking your mind every step of the way.” This is rooted in the American Dream. It’s the essence of this country,” he said.
Ramaswamy also talked the future of AI, the importance of education, and what the next generation will be tackling. Plus, he added that “Capitalism is a unifying force. It’s what brings us together.”
When asked if he would run for the Oval Office again, the Ohio native was quick to say that he is focused on what he can do in this state. “Running for president was the ultimate entrepreneurial journey,” he noted.
But his best advice to the young entrepreneurs in the audience. “Be ambitious and be humble.” He admits it’s a hard combination, but it’s “rocketfuel for success.”
Hollywood Redefined: Winning The Streaming Era Of Entertainment
Americans spent a whopping 12 trillion minutes streaming entertainment content last year, according to Nielsen, a number that translates into 23 million years—and tens of billions of dollars. Netflix alone generated $39 billion in revenue in 2024, and with virtually every streamer in the market raising their prices in 2025, the battle for Americans’ wallets and eyeballs is hotter than ever.
Forbes’ Associate Editor of Under 30, Alexandra York sat down with some of Hollywood’s most up-and-coming stars—Anna Cathcart, Keyla Monterosso Mejia and Marissa Bode—to talk about how they’re navigating the landscape.
One of their key concerns? AI, and how new technology might transform the way movies and television shows are made.
“Hopefully I’m still here in five years,” quipped Monterosso Mejia, before noting that when she got into film, the industry was already in the process of a lot of change: COVID, masks, and social distancing. She started her career on Curb Your Enthusiasm, and went on to roles in Abbot Elementary, One Of Them Days, and more.
One way to boost her brand is through social media, which Monterosso Mejia said made her nervous at first (she didn’t want audiences to bully her) but which she’s come to see as a way to connect with fans and establish her own persona.
Marissa Bode is an American actress and activist. She is the first wheelchair user to play Nessarose Thropp (Elphaba’s sister) in the movie musical Wicked (2024), the highest grossing musical adaptation of all time. The movie was her feature film debut—kickstarting her career along costars like Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo.
“Sometimes I need to remind myself just to take a breath between everything,” said Bode of her best learning while working on Wicked. Bode also talked about her social media presence and how she uses her platform as a space to connect with fans. It’s a place for her to show her “silly side,” and to speak about causes she cares about.
Anna Cathcart is an award-winning Canadian actress who took the spotlight at 14. She played Kitty Song-Covey in the Netflix hit series, To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before (2018) and XO, Kitty (2023). While she is likely best known for her rom-com roles, she was also in the Disney series Descendants (2015), Descendants 2 (2017), and PBS’s Odd Squad. Cathcart talked about learning the ropes of the acting industry at such a young age, and how she was forced to teach herself the nuances of film: Even the trivial things: like “10-1” means bathroom break.
With an eye on the future—and with multiple roles across streaming networks—Cathcart emphasized the beauty of the streaming economy. Shows are reaching people they may not have in the past, she said. Monterroso Mejia agreed that more actors are finding work thanks to the volume of streaming projects, too.
The group also discussed the ability to break into the industry–and how there aren’t rules. You can go viral on TikTok overnight and land gigs the next day, they agreed.
Vibe Check: How To Market To Gen Z Customers In The Digital Age
So much for Gen Z being the broke generation: This group’s spending power is expected to hit $12 trillion by 2030, according to NIQ’s global report on Gen Z.
Zoya Hasan, Under 30 reporter at Forbes, sat down with creators and cofounders to discuss the power the generation holds and what all founders can do to better attract Gen Z consumers to their businesses.
“You don’t know what to believe in anymore, but the one thing you can believe is in relationships and people,” said Amy Liu, the founder and CEO of Tower 28 Beauty, a clean makeup company designed for sensitive skin. She noted that for all the power of online marketing, it’s the person-to-person relationships that have helped her products get sold. Liu told the audience about how her brand (which is sold direct-to-consumer and at retailers including Sephora) has grown through word of mouth through sleepovers—teen girls experiment with makeup and then tell their moms about what’s cool.
Katie Fang knows this from her work as a beauty creator on TikTok, where she shares beauty tips and life updates. “I am raw and real,” Fang said, noting that she only recently realized just how much her digital influence extends to the real world. (Liu affirmed this observation, recounting seeing Fang outside of a Brandy Melville store and a swarm of young girls attempting to talk to her.)
On the subject of influence, Avante Price, cofounder and CEO of Posh, an event management company and marketing platform, advised the audience to be careful about which types of advice and influence they let permeate their brains. “Make sure that your own intuition and own internal voice is louder than the voices around you,” he said.
When Hasan asked the panel for advice for the young entrepreneurs in the room, Liu said “you have to offer a solution to something that exists.” And you have to “do it for yourself.”
“Do what you love and the money will follow,” Price concluded.
The Poppi Playbook: How To Build And Sell A Billion Dollar Business
Poppi is an American success story: The company, which sells prebiotic sodas that are low sugar and low calorie, launched in 2018. By 2023, sales were over $100 million. And in May of this year, PepsiCo acquired the brand for $1.95 billion.
Allison Ellsworth, the cofounder and brand advisor of Poppi, sat down with Forbes’ Editor-at-Large Maneet Ahuja to discuss her up-and-coming beverage brand. “We are one of the fastest growing beverages in the history of beverages,” Ellsworth claimed. Poppi’s biggest competitors are other healthier-sodas like Olipop and Culture Pop, along with more mainstream soda brands like Coca-Cola and Pepsi. But, as of this past May, Poppi sold roughly 3.3 million cans per month on Amazon, making it the #1 best-selling soda on the platform. And PepsiCo saw power in Ellsworth’s growing consumer base.
Ellsworth’s takeaway on what she would do differently if she was to start Poppi all over again: “Get on TikTok and talk about your brand… All it costs is time.”
Beyond The Bottom Line: Unlocking Investment for Impact
Can you do well by also doing good? Steven Bertoni, Assistant Managing Editor of Founders at Forbes sat down with Jonathan Lord, the cofounder and CTO of Flux Marine, and Katherine Sizov, the founder and CEO of Strella, to find out.
Flux Marine is an electric boat motor company that Lord founded after studying mechanical and aerospace engineering at Princeton. The company's design fills a niche in the industry: an option other than combustion motors for boats. Lord reminisced on his rowing days and seeing the thin film of oil in the water that had leaked from boats. “It didn’t have to be like this,” he said Monday.
Through Strella and her team of scientists and engineers, Sizov is finding data-driven solutions for food supply chains. Strella helps suppliers monitor food ripeness levels to determine when the produce should be sold. Today, nearly 40% of our food is wasted, a statistic Sizov is trying to change.
Bertoni turned to Sizov and asked her about the craziest statistic or fact she had about grocery stories or the food industry. “An apple in the grocery story can be over a year old by the time it gets to you,” Sizov said. “They hibernate in the back” until a store decides to place it on the shelves.
Turning Content Into Consumers: Using Social Media To Forge A Business Empire
As of right now, there are five billion social media users worldwide. And the average person spends nearly 2.5 hours a day on the major social media platforms. Ad spending is projected to hit $276 billion and engagement is only increasing. Over 60% of the world’s population uses social media, according to a digital marketing study by Statista.
Many founders and CEOs are finding that a presence on social media can help a growing company, and Forbes’ Alexandra York sat down with two such entrepreneurs. Emily Oberg, the founder of Sporty & Rich, and Claudia Sulewski, the founder and creative director of CYKLAR.
Sporty & Rich is a luxury sportswear brand that originally began as an Instagram moodboard. Before long, Oberg began selling pieces to her audience. The company has grown into a multi-million dollar business. “People want to be part of your world,” Oberg explained—but also said that this was not the mindset she started with. “I don’t know if I’m equipped,” she remembers thinking.
Where Oberg built from scratch, CYKLAR founder Sulewski had a built-in audience from her years on Instagram. She turned that audience into customers for CYKLAR’s products, which she says uses advanced ingredients, nutrient-rich formulas, botanicals and luxurious fragrances to take care of the body, the skin, and its senses. Sulewski said that when developing products she focuses on textures that transform skin routines and turn daily care into a ritual of self rejuvenation.
“I self-funded the first launch,” Sulewski said on Monday. It’s a “huge sacrifice.” But, with a well-established social platform, she felt like she had the support to grow.
Life Lessons From The World’s Youngest Self-Made Woman Billionaire
Lucy Guo returned to the Under 30 stage Monday (after her rousing DJ set Sunday night) for an interview with Chase Peterson-Withorn, a senior editor at Forbes. Today, Guo stands as one of six self-made women billionaires in the world–under the age of 40. She’s the only one who made most of her fortune from a company she left years ago. (In 2016, Lucy Guo cofounded Scale AI with Alexandr Wang. The San Francisco startup took off and the pair made Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list in 2018. But the same year, Wang fired Guo; however, she hung onto her stake in the company and still owns just under 5% of the company.)
On Monday, Guo told Peterson-Withorn that her drive to make money began at an early age: “I started creating my own websites in the third grade,” she said. “I figured out how to make money on my own,” Guo said, recalling that “internet money” was appealing because it was income her parents couldn’t take away (as punishment).
Guo recounted how her parents "weren't happy” when she dropped out of school to pursue a Thiel Fellowship (“Education gave my parents everything they have in life,” she explained), but they now understand that “there’s a different path for success.”
To that point, Guo encouraged the young entrepreneurs in the audience to reach out to mentors, funders, and investors. “Everyone wants to help kids,” she said.
To wrap up their conversation, Peterson-Withorn asked the famously frugal Guo if she will ever stop chasing UberEats deals and lean into her status as one of the world’s wealthiest women.
“I’m Asian,” Guo replied. “It’s a game… I get excited getting free things!”
Balancing Act: Building An Empire Across Sports And Business
Six-time Olympic medalist Suni Lee joined the Under 30 stage Monday afternoon to share her best advice for success. The American gymnast was the 2020 Olympic all-around gold medalist; in 2021, Lee was named the Female Athlete of the Year by Sports Illustrated. She went on to be a part of the “Golden Girls” gymnastic team that won gold at the 2024 Summer Olympics. For Lee, it was a remarkable comeback after battling severe kidney issues before the Games.
After her Olympic success, Lee joined “Dancing With The Stars.” She has also secured partnerships with Lululemon, HOKA, and American Eagle Outfitters. She also stepped into professional broadcasting, interviewing players at the 2025 NBA Draft.
“I’ve tried to take every opportunity,” Lee told Forbes’ Alexandra York. “As long as it’s authentic.” Lee explained how her personal team helps decide which deals to say yes to and which deals to pass on. Lee talked about building the “perfect team… Those are the people who will be there.” Lee was quick to say that the “most important person on my team is my therapist.”
“The goal has been to inspire others… I never wanted the money or the fame,” said Lee. She talked about gymnastics as her “outlet,” and how she likes keeping realms of her life separate. Friends don’t ask her much about gymnastics, because they know it will make her stressed. Lee talked about her relationship with her family, and how she spends more time with her coaches than her parents. "My parents never pushed me. This has always been my dream.”
How To Break The Internet: Commanding Attention In The Always-On Economy
Getting–and keeping–the attention of Gen Z is hard. There are so many distractions, pulling us in every direction. Steven Bertoni sat down with Brianna LaPaglia (known also by her stage name, Brianna Chickenfry), a media personality and cultural commentator, along with Josh Richards, a Canadian entrepreneur and creator, for a deep discussion on the internet and how creators and entrepreneurs can make it work for them.
“You need that TikTok side,” said Richards, one of the top-earning TikTokers, bringing in roughly $5 million each year, thanks to different sponsorships. He talks about building community and influence and how you can monetize aspects of social media. “TikTok is the platform everyone is using,” Richards said. For his longer content (5 minutes to an hour and a half), he will use YouTube, but even then, he will direct back to his TikTok account. Attention spans are so short. Richards emphasized that “you have to understand what your viewers want to see.”
LaPaglia agreed. “It is really hard to grow anywhere else,” she said about TikTok. Beyond constantly posting, LaPaglia explained how to create a “hook” and a “click” that encourages her followers to keep viewing her content. Another piece of advice she gave: have your audience come back for part two. Series are a great way to build loyal followers.
LaPaglia is best known for her Barstool Sports personality. The podcaster uses social media to break down college life and partying. But she was thrown into the spotlight after her breakup with singer-songwriter Zach Bryan and her reaction to the NDA he offered her. She tells her story of reclaiming and rebuilding her life.
Josh Richards and Brianna Chickenfry will rejoin the Under 30 stage for a live recording of their hit podcast, “BFFs,” Tuesday at 3pm.
Climate Catalysts: How Activism Is Driving The Next Wave Of Entrepreneurship
Now more than ever, protecting the Earth is a priority. Social media has helped spread awareness about climate change and bring people together. Dan Alexander, a Senior Editor at Forbes sat down with Xiye Bastida, the cofounder and executive director of the Re-Earth Initiative, and Jerome Foster, a social entrepreneur and Tree Equity Ambassador at American Forests. He is focused on the lack of trees in low income communities.
“Technology has to be an ally to communities,” said Foster. He addressed the common assumption that technology is displacing nature. Foster emphasized the importance of elevating technology, and making social impact more than just a marketing campaign.
Xiya Bastida returned to the Forbes stage Monday (she received the Young Changemaker Award at the Forbes 30/50 Summit in 2024) to talk about her mission to make the climate movement accessible to all. Bastida focuses on Gen Z and how this generation is the architect of the future, ready to take on the crisis with hope, optimism, resilience, and joy–not rage.
“I used to hate the question of what are you going to do when you grow up? Thinking, why do we have to wait to grow up to do things, to change things?” Bastida said. She emphasized how voices in the climate sector are going to become “a lot more important,” especially as we continue to learn more about the environment and adapt to the changing world.
“Everything that we make, everything that we do, is going to be dictated by the climate,” Bastida said, a warning to the crowd.
Old, New Again: How To Make Millions Reviving Beloved Products
In a world where new products instantly appear on shelves and on our “for you” pages, we are constantly consuming. It’s hard to keep track of the products we like and don’t like, because we’re inundated with new trends.
Maneet Ahuja sat down with three entrepreneurs who are innovating older products for this age of new: Troy Bonde, the cofounder and CEO of Sauz, Jeni Britton, the founder and CEO of Floura and the founder of Jeni’s Splendid Ice Creams, and Andy Sauer, the CEO of Garage Beer.
Bonde built Sauz with his best friend and business partner Winston Alfieri. They liked the bright colors and happy energy they felt while walking down the beverage aisle at Whole Foods, but they couldn’t say the same about their walk through the pasta section... They wanted to bring bold flavors and more appealing labels to pasta. It was time for a refresh. They were convinced consumers would not only agree with them but also be receptive to the new look. Gen Z flocked to standout designs and a pop of color. Sauz has almost hit $20 million in sales.
Jeni Britton, the mastermind behind Jeni’s Ice Cream, a brand known for its complex flavors and creamy texture, opened up about problems the company experienced at the beginning of the building process. “We made a lot of mistakes,” she admitted to the weakness of the business model: selling ice cream at a higher price point. It would be easy for another company to sell a similar product for just a little bit less. “We figured it out over time,” Britton said. She talked about the struggle of getting products on shelves: “It can be years to get back on.”
Britton talked about grocery stories at large: “The whole food system needs reinventing.” She says they did that with ice cream. Britton encouraged the audience to “see the opportunity in every room.” That is definitely what Andy Sauer did. In 2024, he brought on the Kelce brothers. “Jason is a product quality fanatic… And has the passion for connecting with consumers,” Sauer said. As the CEO of Garage Beer, he has seen the company hit a valuation of $200 million.
“The party was already started, [the Kelce brothers] just kind of told everybody the address,” said Sauer on Monday afternoon.
Andy Sauer’s three pieces of advice for building a beer brand:
- “Know who your consumer is”
- “Nail your product”
- “Connect in a way that makes the consumer want to come back”
To wrap up the conversation, Ahuja asked the panelists for advice they would give the young entrepreneurs in the audience. Britton emphasized “trusting your gut”—literally. She said trusting her gut sharpened her instincts. Even when trusting her gut was a mistake, she learned from it, and your gut is “more right than wrong.”
All three panelists emphasized the importance of building stories and creating a product that anyone can love.
Beyond The Hype: How Top VC Hemant Taneja Is Investing Billions In The AI Revolution
During the last panel of the day, Steven Bertoni sat down with Hemant Taneja, the CEO and managing director of General Catalyst, a venture capital firm with $36 billion in assets under management. Born in Delhi, Taneja immigrated to the United States when he was 15.
Taneja has been on the Forbes Midas List of top tech investors. He has backed billion-dollar companies like Stripe, Snap, and Canva. The founder–and author–talked about his path: from entrepreneur to running the firm, and the power of AI.
“A lot of intelligence is just sitting on the internet,” Taneja said. When implementing technology into business models, there should be momentum. And there needs to be trust. “Building trust of customers” is crucial for the development of the company, Taneja said. Customers need to trust that they’re getting the best product. And the product needs to be durable, able to withstand the changes of the industry.
“This moment in time, the decisions we’re making, the companies we’re building are going to impact the world for centuries to come.” Taneja said.
Bertoni asked Taneja about CEOs building teams and entrepreneurs looking for cofounders. “We look for excellence,” the venture capitalist said. His goal for General Catalyst is to make it the world’s top investment and transformation company. He is determined to support global resilience through applied AI.
With Monday coming to a close, thank you for tuning in. Save this link for a rundown on tomorrow’s events. Usual programming will continue after the service initiatives kick off. The next conversations will start with AI, what the future holds, and what this means for entrepreneurs.
DAY 2
Welcome Back
Welcome back for day two! While some are volunteering with the Under 30 Service Day team, we will jump into even more conversations around AI: the innovation shaping every industry and the lives of our generation. The conversations feature the brightest minds in the industry: from the Forbes Under 30 AI list to the leaders from the Forbes AI 50 list. We will discuss, debate and demo the future of AI across business, culture, health, entertainment, social impact and more. To end the day, we will continue to hear from some of the leading voices in media, film, sports and retail.
Under 30 Service Day
We’ll gave back to the Columbus community with a half-day of service. There were various Service Day activities.
Helping Hands At Franklinton Prep
Franklinton Prep High School is a public, charter school that operates as a drop-out prevention program for students aged 15-22 who need a second or third chance at earning their high school diploma. The programs provide students with a career readiness curriculum focused in the fields of business, healthcare or construction, then provides graduates with a robust career navigation program to help them launch into the sector in which they trained. This service project addressed the chronic lack of food in the school’s surrounding community, by constructing and installing “blessing boxes” around the neighborhood, which will be stocked with food and hygiene supplies for any community member who needs them. Volunteers worked side-by-side with career tech students, while mentoring and advising the students on career prospects and future goals.
Speed Mentoring At The Keenan Center For Entrepreneurship
Ohio State University’s Keenan Center For Entrepreneurship aims to inspire, engage and empower student entrepreneurs in their endeavors to change the world. Forbes Under 30 Lister volunteers rotated through small groups of students from the Keenan Center, sharing a bit of their backstory and journey to success and helping the aspiring entrepreneurs visualize their goals and dreams. Volunteers gave advice to students and discussed next steps they can take toward accomplishing their entrepreneurial goals.
Hackathon For Expanding Literacy Programs Nationwide
2nd & 7 is a Columbus-based organization that has established youth reading programs in 26 states across the country since its founding in 1999 by three former Ohio State Buckeye football players. The program has provided 800,000 free books and positive role models to kids in need while encouraging young athletes of the community to pay it forward. For this Under 30 Summit Service Day activity, roughly 30 volunteers participated in a hackathon with the 2nd & 7 leadership team to ideate solutions to some of the organization’s goals for growth.
Pathways To Tech: Professional Development Day For Tech Students
Students from three Columbus-based organizations—Color Coded Labs, Per Scholas and NCUS TEC—gathered for a professional development day designed to help job seekers in tech sharpen their professional skills. We kicked off with a short panel session for select volunteers to share their career journeys and highlight the biggest opportunities and challenges in tech. Volunteers then split into two groups, where they took part in mock interviews with students to help them practice their interviewing techniques in a low-pressure environment, and the other group conducted LinkedIn profile reviews, offering personalized tips to optimize profiles, that will only help expand professional networks and attract potential employers. We ended with a networking session for volunteers to provide one-on-one advice and share their tips for success.
Nourishment And Connection At Columbus State
The Mid-Ohio Market at Columbus State Community College is a store for low-income students and community members to access free, fresh and shelf-stable food on a regular basis. It is located on the college’s campus in downtown Columbus. For this Under 30 Summit Service Day activity, 10 volunteers spent one hour in the store stocking nonperishable food items for the next day’s shoppers, then spent one hour networking in-person with student ambassadors whose professional interests align with the concept.
Besa/Freedom A La Cart
Freedom A La Cart is a Columbus nonprofit with a mission to empower survivors of sex trafficking and exploitation to build lives of freedom and self-sufficiency. Through its catering and cafe social enterprise, Freedom A La Cart provides a safe and restorative place for survivors to heal, learn and grow.
This unique service activity combined mentorship and hands-on experience. After a brief introduction and training from the Freedom A La Cart team, volunteers split into two groups. One group provided one-on-one mentorship, resume advice, and career guidance to Freedom A La Cart Workforce Development program participants, while the second group worked in the catering area to learn hands-on what it takes to operate the social enterprise. After lunch, volunteers switched roles in order to get the full experience.
Role Model Reading Program With 2nd & 7
2nd & 7 is a Columbus-based organization that has established youth reading programs in 26 states across the country since its founding in 1999 by three former Ohio State Buckeye football players. The program has provided 800,000 free books and positive role models to kids in need while encouraging young athletes of the community to pay it forward. For this Under 30 Summit Service Day activity, up to 20 volunteers visited Highland Elementary School in the Columbus School District. The volunteers split into four classrooms for a 45-minute session meeting and reading books with 2nd- and 3rd-grade students, discussing the life lessons introduced in the book, and distributing copies of the book to each student as a keepsake (courtesy of 2nd & 7).
AI Innovator Spotlight: All-American Drones For Good
The founder and CEO of BRINC Drones, Blake Resnick, kicks us off. The former Under 30 lister was only 18 years old when he founded BRINC, which manufactures and sells drones for first responders. This technology gives them an extra pair of eyes and ears, especially in places that are too difficult or dangerous to reach. The whole point of this thing is to add space,” Resnick said on Tuesday morning. “I want the drone to arrive before teams.”
The company has raised roughly $82 million and is valued at over $300 million. It’s the “world’s largest public safety drone company,” said the BRINC CEO, who added that “15% of the SWAT teams in the country are actively using this.” Its drones are now used by more than 700 agencies across 50 cities, he said.
Forbes’ Zoya Hasan and Resnick broke down the difficulties in fundraising: “I failed to fundraise," Resnick said before reminiscing on one of his first fundraising calls–with a shirtless TikToker in bed with another guy. That didn’t yield an investment, but it did lead him to Sam Altman, who ultimately backed the company.
BRINC’s drones have some features that set them apart from competition: For example, their drones have been reengineered to flip itself back over if it falls and their cameras point to the horizon, not down (which can be perceived as aggressive). All the drones–and every part–are made in America. “This was really hard to do,” he said. But he had no other choice. The CEO has been “sanctioned by China… I can’t enter that country anymore.”
Resnick also explained how drones can help with a perennial problem: 911 is flooded with nuisance calls. The drones can help public safety officials ascertain these types of calls before resources are directed towards them. Additionally, the software gives more information before teams have arrived at emergencies, enabling them to plan a response.
AI Is Changing The Future Of Work: Are You Ready?
For our next AI talk this morning, Rowan Cheung, the founder and CEO of The Rundown joined Trace Johnson, the cofounder and president of AI OWL, Kiara Nirghin, the cofounder of Chima, and Steven Bertoni, Assistant Managing Editor of Founders at Forbes.
Cheung has built one of the world’s largest newsletters about AI, The Rundown, which has over 1 million active subscribers. He’s interviewed tech giants like Mark Zuckerberg and the CEOs of Google DeepMind and Microsoft. Cheung broke down how he grew a business at the intersection of media and technology.
“Learning how to learn is another skill that should be learned,” said Cheung. “I’m not that great in front of the camera,” he admitted. Though Cheung realized that his audience wanted to see a video component with the content his team pushes out, getting on camera was a hassle. “Doing my hair takes time away from being a founder,” he said. So instead, The Rundown uses AI with his image and automated voiceovers to provide video for its 150 thousand Instagram followers.
Trace Johnson has invented everything from sensor technologies to water recycling systems, pushed by the question: “How can you do what you do even better?” he said. Over the past three years, Johnson has successfully added AI to software models and manufactured housing methods-across industrial environments worldwide–which has boosted their efficiency and productivity. Born in Newark, Ohio, he is committed to helping his home state and has been. by Governor Mike DeWine to the Executive Order of the Ohio Commodores.
Kiara Nirghin and her sister Nikhara cofounded Chima, which builds “human reasoning” AI tools. “AI is going to compete with the time you have,” she said. The software is made to tackle daily business tasks, such as writing an email, or editing images. Chima has raised $5 million in funding from a range of investors, including Y Combinator and Hemant Taneja’s General Catalyst. (Scroll up for a recap on Taneja’s interview with Steven Bertoni.)
“The pace of innovation is happening so fast… The muscle to be productive in the workplace is completely changing,” Nirghin said. “You’re probably already behind.” But, there is good news. “There’s probably never been a better time to be reading and engaged in this space than there is today,” Nirghin said.
Allies In AI: How Startups And Enterprises Win Together
Forbes’ Zoya Hasan sat down with Soyoung Lee, cofounder and head of business development at TwelveLabs. Lee has been crucial in securing over $100 million in funding for the startup, which uses AI to analyze video for key insights and data. In her role, she has helped form partnerships with industry powerhouses like NVIDIA and AWS. Lee broke down how she is leading a global company and shaping the future of ethical AI.
“Video is so important… Video is in every industry,” said Lee. But it can be hard to know which customers are a best fit for her company’s tools. Lee reminisced on moments after conferences when she would race to find founders, just so she could pitch to them, for even a moment. “You need to knock on many, many doors.” As video becomes more ubiquitous, she said there are many ways customers not only use them in their workflows, but also extract key insights from them. But attracting customers means doing a little homework in order to “find the right person at the right organization,” Lee said.
Fun fact: “We like to name our models after horses,” Lee said.
Sparking A New Creativity Explosion
For our next panel, Forbes’ Alex York welcomed Victor Perez, cofounder and CEO of Krea, and Zoe Wrenn, the founder and CEO of Tamber, to the stage. Victor Perez was on this year’s Forbes Next Billion-Dollar Startups list for his design tool, which was built by a team of musicians, poets, designers and videographers. He created a space where artists can access a range of AI models that can generate new images from text prompts, refine existing ones, and even enhance videos. Krea has brought in over 20 million accounts across the globe (including users from Lego, Pixar and Microsoft). The startup has raised $83 million and its estimated revenue is $5 million. His focus is not just “generating” AI but rather creating a tool that lets you manipulate this technology.
Wrenn is a self-taught coder. Through AI-driven software, she built a song (“Hailey”) in 2020, which rocketed to No.2 on Billboard’s Digital Chart and has been played more than 30 million times. Her software has since been updated with eight proprietary machine learning models and is now used by artists all over the world. Users can play around with melodies, get help brainstorming lyrics, and there are also capabilities that allow self-production. Tamber has attracted investors like M13 and Rachhouse VC, and has secured $3 million in funding.
Wrenn started her journey into learning coding by “falling down rabbit holes,” she said. She “went to YouTube, which is the people’s college in my opinion.” Wren explained how it can be hard to learn about computer science and coding in an academic setting. “A lot of the existing models are very old or academic.”
She also talked about the challenges in fundraising that come from being an unconventional founder. “I have blue hair,” she said. So she needed “ people who understand the vibes and the vision.” She emphasized the importance of not taking funds from someone or a team who might not be the best fit.
Both panelists focused on the importance of building a team that is using the software. Too many times non-artists are running music companies, which makes it harder to meet customer needs. “I’m the founder, but I’m also the beta tester,” Wrenn said. “I want to find the pain points.”
Artificial Investing: What Today’s Top VCs Are Looking For In AI Startups
Forbes’ Chase Peterson-Withorn sat down with Will McKelvey from Lerer Hippeau, and Jahanvi Sardana, a partner at Index Ventures. McKelvey leads an early-stage venture capital fund with over $1.2 billion assets under management. Sardana helps lead Index’s cybersecurity and enterprise software investments. As an immigrant woman investor, she is focused on backing outsiders and mission-driven businesses.
McKelvey shared his insights into what makes a great entrepreneur. “The best founders say ‘I don’t know this, but this is how I’m going to figure it out,’” McKelvey said. These founders have a “dripping sense of will to win.” McKelvery also observed that AI is taking some family businesses full circle: it’s the sons of carpenters creating AI tools to make their father’s work more efficient.
“A vast majority of founders shouldn’t be venture-backed,” McKelvey continued. He said you can tell when a founder has what it takes.
Sardana explained the importance of looking far and wide when building a team. Great additions can be found anywhere–you shouldn’t be limited to Silicon Valley or New York City: “Talent is global. Capital is global. Distribution is global. So why should founders not be?” Sardana said her team invests “in a founder first mindset.” And for success in the AI industry, “the only real mode is speed, since there’s a new AI model every week.
“There is a lot that’s going to change, but the founder is the constant,” Sardana said. “This is why we back founders, not businesses.”
Inside The Wild Life Of A Top Creator
Jake Shane started to gain traction on Instagram in 2021 by rating octopus dishes at restaurants, a fame he has parlayed into a recent 36-city comedy tour, including Radio City in New York. His podcast, “Therapuss,” hosts major celebrities, like Katy Perry, Tate McRae, and Glen Powell. He also uses the platform to give life advice to listeners. In 2023, he went viral on TikTok for his funny reenactments of historical events. Shane has made both our 30 Under 30 list as well as our Top Creators list.
This afternoon, Shane was given a warm welcome as he walked out onto the stage with Forbes’ Steven Bertoni. They jumped into the “unchartered territory of advertising” that faces creators on social platforms. Shane broke down the difficulty of working with brands and making sure that goals are aligned. If a brand has limitations on which words can be used, that might not align with the creator’s audience. “You need to make it sound authentic to what the creator’s content is,” said Shane. “The only person that knows what the audience wants to see is the creator… You just have to trust yourself.”
“Therapuss” is approaching its 100th show. “I can’t believe I do this for a living,” said Shane. But it didn’t always come easy. “I would push it off in my head,” said Shane, as he talked about the nervousness he felt before stepping onto the stage. But how he got used to it and decided to make it his living: “Being on stage takes you out of that internet haze.”
Game Changers: How Brands Can Leverage The $2 Billion Women's Sports Industry
Forbes’ Alex York sits down with our biggest panel: Cherry Beagles, founder and CEO of The 400 Club; Talia Bender, president of The Female Quotient; Jacie deHoop, cofounder of The GIST; and Masai Russell, the Olympic Gold Medalist.
Beagles’ 400 Club connects sports brands to female fans through product activations, marketing campaigns and events. The 400 Club also helps female athletes find commercial opportunities. With more than 45 pro athlete members and over 40 female-led brands, the company is valued at $1.7 million. Its clients include Nike, Arsenal FC, Chelsea FC, TikTok and Wimbledon. Beagles’ talked about her experience growing up and how her girlfriends weren’t really focused on athletics: “There is such a huge demographic of women who haven’t yet found their love of sports… We believe every woman is a sports fan, they just don’t know it yet.”
Bender is another Under 30 lister for her work on The Female Quotient, a company aimed at advancing equality in the workplace through marketing and advertising campaigns. Bender oversees programming at more than 60 major annual events, featuring 5,000 leaders. “We are a place where leaders come and convene,” said Bender. She has built relationships with organizations including the Ad Council, Black Girls Code and Cannes Lions See It Be It.
The GIST is working to change the amount of time and coverage female athletes get in sports media. Right now, it’s roughly 4%. The GIST was built to change exactly that. deHoop is one of three founders. The trio created a sports newsletter for women, which has over 50,000 subscribers, and lists Soul Cycle and Lululemon as brand partners.
deHoop talked about the struggle of getting the attention of investors. “A few years ago, it was a different time,” she said. Luckily, women's sports has taken a more prominent position on the stage, but back then her team was running on faith. “You have to be a little bit delusional when starting your company… It was hard. It has been a journey.”
GIST’s deHoop also talked about building her team and bringing in millions of “gisters.” “Only 14% of sports journalists are women. Our content team is only women,” she said. “I felt like the sports industry was like an old boy’s club.”
Russell won the gold medal in the Women’s 100-meter Hurdles at the 2024 Paris Olympic Games–by just one one-hundredth of a second. She was the first American woman to win gold in this event since 2016. Russell focused on the struggle of identity and how the fans perceive the athlete. “There’s no visibility as a professional.” The gold medalist discussed how many fans think the Olympics are the only focus, the only competition. “It’s every single day,” Russell said.
How Retailers Compete In The Age Of Social Media Shopping
Forbes’ Zoya Hasan came back to the stage for a panel with Danielle Guizio, CEO and designer of GUIZIO, and Kate Ridley, chief brand officer at PMI WW Brands (Stanley 1913). Guizio started her eponymous streetwear fashion brand a little over ten years ago–with only $400 in savings and a line of graphic Ts that instantly sold out. She has since grown her line to affordable shorts, tops, bikinis and more. The brand is a favorite of celebrities like Bella Hadid, Kendall Jenner and Hailey Baldwin. Last year, it opened its flagship store in New York City.
Guizio told the audience that even as CEO, she sometimes lingers outside of changing rooms to either help customers or listen to their immediate–and unfiltered reactions–to her pieces. This allows her brand to not only make more immediate changes, but also get an honest take on customer sentiment.
The founder told the audience to “believe in yourself and be patient… You can achieve anything.” Even when others put you down, “you have to be your biggest cheerleader.”
Both Guizio and Ridley talked about quality control. At Stanley, “our quality is unparalleled. We stand behind our promise,” Ridley said. Even as the TikTok Shop and other online merchants tempt potential buyers to go with their much cheaper knockoff, Ridley believes that protecting your brand and sticking to your mission is what really matters. “We stand behind our community,” Ridley said.
Stanley cups may be all the rage right now, but its brand is over 100 years old. It owes that longevity to the fact that “we are constantly innovating,” Ridley said. Her team is focused on bringing something new each and every day, whether it’s a collaboration, new colors, or new categories.
“Be true to your brand. Be authentic. Define who you are. And don’t mess with it,” Ridley said. The best testament to that dedication, she said, is that those who own her company’s water bottle don’t call it one–they call it a Stanley.
Entrepreneurship Meets Entertainment: Lili Reinhart’s Next Move
For our last panel of the conference we had the beloved Lili Reinhart join Forbes’ Alex York on stage. Reinhart is an actress, producer and founder of Personal Day, a skincare brand inspired by her own acne journey. She’s been in the spotlight since playing Betty Cooper on the CW’s hit series Riverdale. But she has since taken her entertainment career one step further: starring in and acting as the executive producer for romance film Chemical Hearts.
Reinhart didn’t shy away from talking about her struggles with depression and work-life balance. “I want to tell stories about women who are overcoming their depression or anxiety,” said Reinhart. “We are still being pushed into these boxes that I’m not a fan of,” she said, which is why she wants to tell stories about women that transcend stereotypes.
While she’s grateful that throughout Riverdale’s hundred plus episodes, “I got to do quite literally anything and everything someone can do on a show.” Reinhart was candid about the reality of signing a contract that lasts for years, especially at such a young age. “You don’t even realize.”
As an actress, Reinhart has focused on independent film and television making since Riverdale ended. “It’s a lot more hardy, but the subject matter is a lot more interesting to me,” said Reinhart. “It’s what I like to watch.”
Reinhart has also been focused on her skincare brand, which came about when people in the industry came to her and asked, “Do you want to have a brand?”
It was a good fit for her. Since her early days on Riverdale, Reinhart had been vocal about her acne and how it fueled her depression and anxiety. She said she always appreciated when her role models talked about acne–and gave advice. But, she “didn’t want to add products to an overcrowded market” So she decided to stand out by creating a skincare line that doesn’t have acne-inducing ingredients. “I wanted to create something trustworthy.” “I can make a difference and not just throw something out there,” Reinhart said. Personal Day launched last October and its products are in 700 Ulta Beauty stores. When asked about her involvement in the brand, she said that she wants to “know my fan base... I want to make sure I’m speaking to them.” That said, she wants the products to speak for themselves, which is why they don’t use her name..
Each product is under $40 in order to reach younger generations who aren’t able to pay for expensive skincare. In a world where beauty and makeup has taken over corners of the internet, Reinhart wants to protect a space for the girls who still need to focus on their acne. “It’s overlooked,” she said. “I want to make popular products that are acne safe.” Her next product, an acne-treating foam called “Just Like New” launches tomorrow.
And after two great days, our programming has now come to an end! Thank you for reading. Until next year!

headline: DCU New Batman Casting Options Include Actor Who Could Be Best Choice
summary: WBD and DC Studios have big choices to make about how to introduce Batman in their shared cinematic universe. And one actor stands out who could make most everyone happy.
